paper.title: Benchmarking Materials Property Prediction Methods: The Matbench Test Set and Automatminer Reference Algorithm

thesis: A fixed set of tasks and nested cross-validation makes materials-property models comparable, revealing that no single model family dominates every data regime.

nodes.title: How should materials predictors be compared?
nodes.body: Create a reproducible comparison across diverse materials properties without leakage or task-specific split advantages.

nodes.title: Freeze tasks and nested splits
nodes.body: Use source datasets as-is and prescribe consistent nested cross-validation with five outer folds.

nodes.title: Build 13 benchmark tasks
nodes.body: Assemble regression and classification tasks spanning electronic, thermodynamic, mechanical and other materials properties.

nodes.title: Run reference algorithms
nodes.body: Evaluate Automatminer, CGCNN, MEGNet, random forests and dummy baselines under the same split protocol.

nodes.title: Automatminer leads most tasks
nodes.body: The automated classical pipeline achieved the best reported score on eight of thirteen tasks.

nodes.title: Graph networks benefit from scale
nodes.body: Graph neural networks become more consistently competitive on larger datasets, around ten thousand samples and above.

nodes.title: Property type still matters
nodes.body: Formation-energy and phonon-density tasks show task-specific graph-network advantages that sample count alone does not explain.

nodes.title: Standardization exposes conditional winners
nodes.body: A shared benchmark supports fair comparison while showing that model choice depends on dataset size and target property.

openQuestions: The fixture records published aggregate results, not every fold-level prediction or executable environment.
